title: Wider family, birth and marriage
intro: Read plate 4 alongside this unit. Spanish builds in-law words from the base word rather than compounding with in-law, so each one has to be learned separately — and the most dangerous word here is pariente, which does not mean parent.

entries.note: In Spain tío doubles as slang for guy or mate. In Latin America it does not.

ex.es: Mi tía vive en Guadalajara.
ex.en: My aunt lives in Guadalajara.

entries.note: primo hermano is a first cousin; primo segundo a second cousin.

ex.es: Crecí con mis primos en el campo.
ex.en: I grew up with my cousins in the countryside.

ex.es: Le compré un regalo a mi sobrina.
ex.en: I bought my niece a present.

entries.note: los nietos covers grandchildren of either sex.

ex.es: Los abuelos cuidan a sus nietos los viernes.
ex.en: The grandparents look after their grandchildren on Fridays.

entries.note: bis- adds a generation each time: bisnieto is a great-grandchild.

ex.es: Mi bisabuela llegó de Polonia en 1930.
ex.en: My great-grandmother arrived from Poland in 1930.

entries.note: los suegros means the in-laws as a pair.

ex.es: Mis suegros vienen a cenar el domingo.
ex.en: My in-laws are coming to dinner on Sunday.

ex.es: Su cuñado le consiguió el trabajo.
ex.en: His brother-in-law got him the job.

entries.note: Two unrelated words rather than a matched pair — these two simply have to be memorised.

ex.es: Su nuera es arquitecta.
ex.en: Her daughter-in-law is an architect.

entries.warn: A false friend, and a costly one. Parents is los padres. Mis parientes means my relatives — cousins, aunts, the lot.

ex.es: Tengo parientes en tres países.
ex.en: I have relatives in three countries.

entries.note: Reflexive, and the person you marry takes con: se casó con Ana. estar casado is to be married.

ex.es: Se casaron en la playa.
ex.en: They got married on the beach.

entries.note: el matrimonio is the marriage itself, the institution, not the party.

ex.es: La boda fue pequeña y bonita.
ex.en: The wedding was small and lovely.

entries.note: Goes with ser, not estar: es soltera.

ex.es: Sigue soltero y muy contento.
ex.en: He's still single and very happy.

entries.note: One word, not a passive. Only the yo form is irregular.

ex.es: Nací en Jerusalén.
ex.en: I was born in Jerusalem.

ex.es: El árbol creció muy rápido.
ex.en: The tree grew very fast.

ex.es: Crecí en un pueblo chico.
ex.en: I grew up in a small town.

entries.note: Past participle is muerto. morirse de risa is to die laughing.

ex.es: Su abuelo murió el año pasado.
ex.en: His grandfather died last year.

entries.note: Masculine whatever the baby is: el bebé es una niña.

ex.es: El bebé durmió toda la noche.
ex.en: The baby slept all night.

entries.note: Plural jóvenes takes an accent, because the stress must stay on the first syllable.

ex.es: Es demasiado joven para manejar.
ex.en: He's too young to drive.

ex.es: Los jóvenes se reúnen en la plaza.
ex.en: The young people gather in the square.

entries.note: Blunt about people — mayor is the polite word. mis viejos for my parents is warm, not rude, in Mexico and the Southern Cone.

ex.es: Ese carro ya está muy viejo.
ex.en: That car is very old now.

ex.es: Voy a visitar a mis viejos.
ex.en: I'm going to visit my folks.

entries.note: Already ends in -s in the singular and does not change in the plural: un cumpleaños, dos cumpleaños.

ex.es: ¡Feliz cumpleaños!
ex.en: Happy birthday!

entries.note: Most Spanish speakers carry two: the father's first, then the mother's. García Márquez is one person, not two names.

ex.es: ¿Cómo se escribe su apellido?
ex.en: How do you spell your surname?
